title: Intracranial arteriovenous malformation (AVM) or meningothelial meningioma (MM)? Outlining the similarities and differences on imaging studies for an accurate diagnosis, case report
journal: International Journal of Surgery Case Reports
case_prompt: A young, previously healthy patient presented with a two-week history of severe headache and vomiting that recurred despite transient relief from analgesics and antiemetics. There was no history of trauma, surgery, smoking, drug use, or relevant family history. On examination, vital signs were stable, Glasgow Coma Scale score was 14 (E3, V5, M6), and there were no focal neurologic deficits. Routine blood tests were normal. Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a left parasagittal frontal space-occupying lesion with mass effect, cerebral edema, and asymmetric ventricular enlargement. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a hyperdense lesion measuring approximately 60 × 52 × 38 mm with similar mass effect and edema. Sagittal views revealed the lesion abutting the sphenoid wing. CT angiography revealed multiple enlarged vascular channels and several larger feeding vessels within a vascularized left frontal lesion. Upon radiologic interpretation, these findings were concluded to represent a large left frontal arteriovenous malformation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Arteriovenous malformation was the initial working diagnosis based on CT angiography findings of vascular channels and vessels — “upon interpretation by the radiologists, it was concluded as a large left frontal AVM.”  
2. Meningioma was considered after noting imaging features inconsistent with AVM — “The strong imaging features that were against AVM and were pro MM in our isolated case are: (a) the presence of parenchymal tissue within the vascular network or ‘nidus’, (b) a dural ‘tail’ abutting left greater sphenoid wing and (c) increased vasogenic edema.”
